message.text: Is it always true that the product of two non-identical sets of primes yield distinct integers?

message.title: Matt (Math) · Pack: Sample
message.text:
Yes, it is always true that the product of two non-identical sets of primes yields distinct integers. This is due to the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, which states that every integer greater than 1 is either a prime number itself or can be uniquely represented as a product of prime numbers, up to the order of the factors. 

If you have two different sets of prime numbers, their products will have different prime factorizations. Since the prime factorization of a number is unique, the products of these two different sets of primes will also be different. Therefore, the integers resulting from these products will be distinct.

message.title: You
message.text: Thanks. But based on what you said it seems there must be a one to one mapping between the power set of primes and the set of all integers. Is that right?

message.title: Matt (Math) · Pack: Sample
message.text:
That's an interesting observation! However, it's not quite accurate to say there's a one-to-one mapping between the power set of primes and the set of all integers. 

The power set of primes includes the empty set, which corresponds to the integer 1 (since the product of no primes is defined as 1). Also, the power set of primes contains sets with repeated primes, which would correspond to the same integer (e.g., the set {2, 2} and the set {2} both correspond to the integer 4).

So while there is a relationship between the power set of primes and the set of integers, it's not a one-to-one mapping. Instead, it's a many-to-one mapping, where multiple elements in the power set of primes can correspond to the same integer.

message.title: Matt (Math) · Pack: Sample
message.text:
You're absolutely correct, and I appreciate your attention to detail. Let's clarify this.

The power set of the primes, excluding the empty set, indeed has a one-to-one correspondence with a proper subset of the integers, specifically the positive integers that are products of distinct primes. This is because each non-empty subset of primes corresponds to a unique product of those primes.

However, the power set of the primes has the same cardinality as the set of all integers, not just the positive integers. This is because the power set of any infinite set has a strictly greater cardinality than the set itself. In the case of the primes, the power set includes all possible combinations of primes, including the empty set, which corresponds to the integer 1.

So, while there is an injection from the power set of primes (excluding the empty set) to the positive integers, there is no injection from the power set of primes to the entire set of integers. This is because the power set of the primes is uncountably infinite, while the set of integers is countably infinite.
